warmup.q: PriceList and SeatFinder each take a SeatingPlan in their constructor, and BoxOffice takes both. A ten-line container builds BoxOffice by calling each constructor it finds, after building that constructor's parameters the same way. How many SeatingPlan objects does it create?
options: One: the JVM reuses an object when the same class is asked for twice
Two: one for each constructor that asks for it
Three: one per class in the graph
None until a method is called on SeatingPlan
warmup.why: Recursion with no memory builds a fresh dependency every time a constructor asks for one, so PriceList gets one plan and SeatFinder another. To share one SeatingPlan, the container has to remember what it already made: one stored instance per type. That memory is what a container calls the singleton scope.

opening:
Remember the theatre company from the Class loading track? It sells tickets through a box office program. Before the doors open, the program sets up its parts: a seating plan, a price list, a sales book, and a link to the city's booking service, which holds the seats for every theatre in town. The box office needs all four.

Something has to build those parts in the right order and hand each one what it needs. The easy trap is to let every class build its own helpers with new. It works on the first night. Then the price list and the seat finder, which picks free seats, each make a seating plan of their own, and nobody knows which one is right.

The Startup track ended with a toolbox for starting a program fast. Part 4 now ends with three sittings that build a dependency injection container: a small program that builds your objects and hands each one the other objects it needs, so classes don't build their own helpers. In this sitting, we'll find the parts, read their constructors, order them and build each shared part once. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a box office that built two seating plans for one hall. Now the container reads every card before the doors open. It picks one constructor per part, puts the parts in order, names any loop, and builds each shared part once, however many customers arrive in the same second.

Now look in your own code for a constructor that calls new on a helper, or for a static getInstance() method. Each one is a class building its own seating plan.

Next, we'll have the box office's calls to the booking service timed and retried, without changing a line of BoxOffice. How can a container slip extra work around a method call?

sections.h: What we'll build: a container for the box office, starting with ten lines of reflection
sections.html:
Most programs start with a block like this somewhere near main. Here it sets up the box office:

Java
BookingConfig config = new BookingConfig();
SeatingPlan plan = new SeatingPlan();
BoxOffice office = new BoxOffice(
        new RemoteBookingClient(config),     // talks to the city's booking service
        new PriceList(plan),
        new SalesBook());
Kotlin
val config = BookingConfig()
val plan = SeatingPlan()
val office = BoxOffice(
    RemoteBookingClient(config),             // talks to the city's booking service
    PriceList(plan),
    SalesBook())

That block is dependency injection done by hand. A dependency is an object that another object needs to do its job, and injecting it means handing it in from outside, here through the constructor. BoxOffice never calls new on its helpers, so a test can hand it a fake booking service and never touch the network. The block has two jobs, and both get harder as the program grows. It must build things in the right order: config before the booking client that reads it. And it must share the right objects: one plan for everyone. With six classes you do that in your head. With eighty, someone adds a constructor parameter, and the block stops compiling in three places.

Picture the theatre's front-of-house manager an hour before the doors open. Every desk in the foyer has a card that says what it needs before it can open. The box office card says "the booking link, the price list, the sales book", and the price list's card says "the seating plan". The manager reads every card, sets things out so that nothing opens before what it needs, and puts a single seating plan where everyone can reach it. A container is that manager, written in code, and the cards are the constructors.

The manager makes three decisions for each desk, and so does a container. Which classes take part? We'll call them components. How do you build one? Its constructor says what it needs. How many of each should exist? That's its scope. Over three sittings, we'll build a container that makes all three decisions, as the figure shows. This sitting wires the parts by reflection, the JDK's way of asking a class about itself while the program runs. The next one wraps some parts in proxies, the stand-ins from the Class loading track, to time and retry their calls. The last one measures what all of it costs, then writes the same wiring out before the program starts. Each lab begins with the previous lab's solution, so you can pick up at any sitting.

The smallest container fits in ten lines. type.getConstructors() returns a class's public constructors as Constructor objects. getParameterTypes() lists what one needs, and newInstance(args) calls it, which creates the object and runs the constructor exactly as new would. Build each parameter first, the same way, and you have a container:

Java
static Object build(Class<?> type) throws ReflectiveOperationException {
    Constructor<?> c = type.getConstructors()[0];          // the card: what it needs
    Object[] args = new Object[c.getParameterCount()];
    for (int i = 0; i < args.length; i++) args[i] = build(c.getParameterTypes()[i]);   // build those first
    return c.newInstance(args);                            // then the part itself
}
Kotlin
fun build(type: Class<*>): Any {
    val c = type.constructors[0]                           // the card: what it needs
    return c.newInstance(*c.parameterTypes.map { build(it) }.toTypedArray())   // those first, then the part
}

Read it as one sentence: to build a part, build everything its constructor asks for, then call the constructor. The demo hands it a box office whose PriceList and SeatFinder both need a SeatingPlan. By hand, new SeatingPlan printed once. By reflection it printed twice:

by reflection:
  new SeatingPlan
  new PriceList
  new SeatingPlan
  new SeatFinder
  new BoxOffice

Two seating plans for one hall, and each of them is sure it's the real one. Our ten lines have no memory, so they build a fresh plan for every constructor that asks. That's one of four flaws, and this lesson fixes all of them. The code takes "the first" constructor, when a class may have several. It has no list of the classes that take part. It would loop forever if two cards needed each other. And it builds a shared part once per request instead of once. Let's start with the list.

try.title: Count the seating plans
steps: Read TinyContainerDemo (or the Kotlin twin). PriceList and SeatFinder both need a SeatingPlan. Predict how many times new SeatingPlan prints in each half.

Give build a memory: add static final Map<Class<?>, Object> made = new HashMap<>();, return made.get(type) when it's there, and call made.put(type, result) before returning. In Kotlin, made.getOrPut(type) { ... } does both. Run it again.

code.title: TinyContainerDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.container.l01.demo; import java.lang.reflect.Constructor; /** The smallest container that works: read a constructor, build its parameters first, then call it. */ public class TinyContainerDemo { public static class SeatingPlan { public SeatingPlan() { System.out.println(" new SeatingPlan"); } } public static class PriceList { public PriceList(SeatingPlan plan) { System.out.println(" new PriceList"); } } public static class SeatFinder { public SeatFinder(SeatingPlan plan) { System.out.println(" new SeatFinder"); } } public static class BoxOffice { public BoxOffice(PriceList prices, SeatFinder finder) { System.out.println(" new BoxOffice"); } } static Object build(Class<?> type) throws ReflectiveOperationException { Constructor<?> constructor = type.getConstructors()[0]; // 1. the recipe is the constructor Class<?>[] needs = constructor.getParameterTypes(); Object[] args = new Object[needs.length]; for (int i = 0; i < needs.length; i++) args[i] = build(needs[i]); // 2. build what it needs first return constructor.newInstance(args); // 3. then the object itself } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println("by hand:"); SeatingPlan plan = new SeatingPlan(); new BoxOffice(new PriceList(plan), new SeatFinder(plan)); System.out.println("by reflection:"); build(BoxOffice.class); } }

alt.title: TinyContainerDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.container.l01.demo // The smallest container that works: read a constructor, build its parameters first, then call it. class KSeatingPlan { init { println(" new KSeatingPlan") } } class KPriceList(plan: KSeatingPlan) { init { println(" new KPriceList") } } class KSeatFinder(plan: KSeatingPlan) { init { println(" new KSeatFinder") } } class KBoxOffice(prices: KPriceList, finder: KSeatFinder) { init { println(" new KBoxOffice") } } fun build(type: Class<*>): Any { val constructor = type.constructors[0] // 1. the recipe is the constructor val args = constructor.parameterTypes.map { build(it) } // 2. build what it needs first return constructor.newInstance(*args.toTypedArray()) // 3. then the object itself } fun main() { println("by hand:") val plan = KSeatingPlan() KBoxOffice(KPriceList(plan), KSeatFinder(plan)) println("by reflection:") build(KBoxOffice::class.java) }

try.expect: By hand, new SeatingPlan prints once, because you passed the same plan twice. By reflection it prints twice: once for PriceList and once for SeatFinder. With the map it prints once. That map is a singleton scope in its simplest form, and section 4 shows why the plain version breaks when several threads ask at once.

sections.h: Find the parts: a list you write, or a scan through a class loader
sections.html:
The simplest way to tell a container which classes take part is a list you write: new Container(List.of(BoxOffice.class, SalesBook.class, ...)). A list is fast and plain, and it's one more file to keep in step with the code. The usual alternative is to mark each component with an annotation, a label in the source that tools can read, such as @Component, and then to search for the label.

That search goes through a class loader. A class loader is the props team from Class loading: loaders, delegation, linking and initialization. It fetches each class only when a scene first needs it, and asks its senior first. loader.getResources("workbench/container/l01/demo/app") asks the team where a package's directory is. It answers with one URL for every place on the class path (the list of directories and JAR files the JVM loads classes from) that holds the package. For a build directory it's a file: URL; inside a JAR it's a jar:file:...!/workbench/... URL. You list the .class files there and turn each file name into a class name.

Then you load each class, and one argument decides what runs:

Java
Class<?> c = Class.forName(name, false, loader);           // load and link, no <clinit>
if (c.isAnnotationPresent(Component.class)) components.add(c);
Kotlin
val c = Class.forName(name, false, loader)                 // load and link, no <clinit>
if (c.isAnnotationPresent(Component::class.java)) components += c

false means "fetch the prop and check it, but don't hold its dress rehearsal". The rehearsal is <clinit>, a class's static initializer, the code that sets its static fields, and the JVM runs it once, on the class's first real use. The one-argument Class.forName(name) holds the rehearsal on the spot. In a scan, that runs every static initializer in the package, components or not, before anyone has asked for anything. The demo's package has two classes whose initializers print a line, and with true both lines appear in the middle of the scan:

  AttendanceLog.<clinit>: opening the attendance file
  TicketArchive.<clinit>: loading 40,000 old tickets

The annotation needs one setting too. @Component must carry @Retention(RUNTIME). With the default, CLASS, javac writes the label into the class file, but the JVM never shows it to reflection, so isAnnotationPresent says false and the scan finds nothing. Nothing fails, either. The container just starts empty.

A scan has a price that a list doesn't. It loads every class in the package, including the ones that turn out not to be components. In the demo, scanning an 11-class package loaded 272 classes: the 11, plus the JDK code for listing directories, reading streams and checking annotations. Why the JVM starts slowly, and how to measure it pictured the JVM as a corner shop that unpacks and checks every box each morning: every class it loads is found, read and checked again on every launch. A large program that scans thousands of classes pays for all of them at every start, even for the ones it throws away.

One more trap hides in JAR files. getResources finds a package inside a JAR only when the JAR has an entry for the directory itself. Most build tools write those entries, but a JAR packed with files only gives the scan zero roots. Again nothing fails: the props team simply reports an empty store.

So the lab's container takes a list, and a ClassScanner (given complete) can build that list with forName(name, false, loader). Next, the container must read each card.

try.title: Scan a package, then hold every dress rehearsal by accident
steps: Read ScanDemo (or ScanDemo.kt). TicketArchive and AttendanceLog in the app package print a line from their static initializers.
Predict: does either line print during the scan? Then run it.
Set INITIALIZE = true and run it again. Then read the last two lines: the same package packed into two JAR files.

code.title: ScanDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.container.l01.demo; import workbench.container.l01.Component; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.OutputStream; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.net.URL; import java.net.URLClassLoader; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.List; import java.util.jar.JarEntry; import java.util.jar.JarOutputStream; import java.util.stream.Stream; /** Scans one package for @Component classes, first in a directory, then in two JAR files. */ public class ScanDemo { static final String PACKAGE = "workbench.container.l01.demo.app"; static final boolean INITIALIZE = false; // try true: what does Class.forName(name, true, loader) run? public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { ClassLoader loader = ScanDemo.class.getClassLoader(); String path = PACKAGE.replace('.', '/'); long before = ManagementFactory.getClassLoadingMXBean().getTotalLoadedClassCount(); for (URL root : Collections.list(loader.getResources(path))) { // one URL per class path entry System.out.println("root: ..." + root.toString().substring(root.toString().indexOf("/build/"))); List<String> components = new ArrayList<>(); try (Stream<Path> files = Files.list(Path.of(root.toURI()))) { for (Path f : files.sorted().toList()) { String file = f.getFileName().toString(); if (!file.endsWith(".class")) continue; Class<?> c = Class.forName(PACKAGE + "." + file.replace(".class", ""), INITIALIZE, loader); if (c.isAnnotationPresent(Component.class)) components.add(c.getSimpleName()); } } System.out.println("components: " + components); } long after = ManagementFactory.getClassLoadingMXBean().getTotalLoadedClassCount(); System.out.println("classes loaded during the scan: " + (after - before)); // The same package packed into a JAR twice: with directory entries, and with files only. Path classes = Path.of(ScanDemo.class.getProtectionDomain().getCodeSource().getLocation().toURI()); Path dir = Files.createDirectories(classes.getParent().getParent().getParent().resolve("cap4")); // container/build/cap4 for (boolean withDirectories : new boolean[] {true, false}) { Path jar = pack(classes, path, dir.resolve(withDirectories ? "app-with-dirs.jar" : "app-files-only.jar"), withDirectories); try (URLClassLoader jarLoader = new URLClassLoader(new URL[] {jar.toUri().toURL()}, null)) { List<URL> roots = Collections.list(jarLoader.getResources(path)); System.out.printf("%-18s getResources found %d root(s) %s%n", jar.getFileName(), roots.size(), roots.isEmpty() ? "" : roots.get(0).getProtocol() + ":...!/" + path); } } } static Path pack(Path classes, String path, Path jar, boolean withDirectories) throws IOException { try (OutputStream file = Files.newOutputStream(jar); JarOutputStream out = new JarOutputStream(file)) { if (withDirectories) { // "workbench/", "workbench/container/", ... as entries of their own String prefix = ""; for (String part : path.split("/")) { prefix += part + "/"; out.putNextEntry(new JarEntry(prefix)); out.closeEntry(); } } try (Stream<Path> files = Files.list(classes.resolve(path))) { for (Path f : files.sorted().toList()) { out.putNextEntry(new JarEntry(path + "/" + f.getFileName())); out.write(Files.readAllBytes(f)); out.closeEntry(); } } } return jar; } }

before}") // The same package packed into a JAR twice: with directory entries, and with files only. val packageDir = Path.of(loader.getResource(path)!!.toURI()) val appClasses = path.split("/").fold(packageDir) { dir, _ -> dir.parent } // build/classes/java/demo val dir = Files.createDirectories(appClasses.parent.parent.parent.resolve("cap4")) // container/build/cap4 for (withDirectories in listOf(true, false)) { val jar = pack(appClasses, path, dir.resolve(if (withDirectories) "kt-app-with-dirs.jar" else "kt-app-files-only.jar"), withDirectories) URLClassLoader(arrayOf(jar.toUri().toURL()), null).use { jarLoader -> val roots = jarLoader.getResources(path).toList() println("%-21s getResources found %d root(s) %s".format(jar.name, roots.size, if (roots.isEmpty()) "" else "${roots[0].protocol}:...!/$path")) } } } private fun pack(classes: Path, path: String, jar: Path, withDirectories: Boolean): Path { JarOutputStream(Files.newOutputStream(jar)).use { out -> if (withDirectories) { // "workbench/", "workbench/container/", ... as entries of their own var prefix = "" for (part in path.split("/")) { prefix += "$part/" out.putNextEntry(JarEntry(prefix)) out.closeEntry() } } Files.list(classes.resolve(path)).use { files -> for (f in files.sorted().toList()) { out.putNextEntry(JarEntry("$path/${f.name}")) out.write(Files.readAllBytes(f)) out.closeEntry() } } } return jar }

try.expect: With INITIALIZE = false, no initializer runs. The scan lists nine components (PriceFormat and the BookingClient interface are skipped) and reports 272 classes loaded (200 in the Kotlin run, which had loaded more before it started counting). With true, AttendanceLog.<clinit>: opening the attendance file and TicketArchive.<clinit>: loading 40,000 old tickets print in the middle of the scan, although nothing has asked for either component. The JAR with directory entries gives one jar: root; the files-only JAR gives none.

aside.title: Do real frameworks scan like this?
aside.html: Spring, a widely used framework (a library that creates your program's parts and connects them for you), scans the class path at every start, much as this section does, and reads the annotations with reflection. Quarkus and Micronaut, two newer frameworks, do the scan while the program is being built and write down what they found, so a start reads a ready-made list. Both choices work. They pay the same bill at different times, at every start or once per build, and lesson 3 of this track measures the difference on our box office.

sections.h: Read each card: pick one constructor, then put the parts in order
sections.html:
Every card must be readable, and in code a card is a constructor. A class can have several, and reflection hands them back in no order you can rely on, so "the first" is a coin toss. The lab's rule is the one most containers use. If exactly one public constructor carries @Inject, use it. If the class has only one public constructor, use that. Otherwise refuse, with a message that says what to do: TwoDoors has 2 public constructors; mark the one to use with @Inject.

Kotlin makes "only one public constructor" harder than it looks. Write class PriceList(val plan: SeatingPlan, val feePercent: Int = 3), and the JVM sees two public constructors: yours, and a synthetic one, made by the compiler rather than by you, that takes an extra int and a DefaultConstructorMarker. Kotlin callers use it when they leave feePercent out. It's the $default trick that Reading bytecode: javap, the operand stack and Kotlin's output found in the prompt book's shorthand, applied to a constructor. The container skips it with isSynthetic(). When every parameter has a default, kotlinc adds a third, a real no-argument constructor, and in this track's run it copied @Inject onto that one too. The container then sees two marked constructors and refuses. The cure is simple: don't give injected parameters defaults.

Each parameter is matched by its type, never by its name. A class file keeps parameter names only when javac runs with -parameters (-java-parameters for kotlinc), so reflection usually reports arg0 and arg1. The type is always there. A parameter of interface type, such as BookingClient, goes to the one component that implements it, here RemoteBookingClient. None, or two, is an error.

Now the order. Visit a component, visit everything its constructor needs, and only then add the component to the list. That's a depth-first, post-order walk: depth first because it follows one card's needs all the way down before it moves on, and post-order because a component joins the list after its needs. The result is a creation order, a list in which every component comes after everything it depends on. A shared part joins once, because the walk skips anything already done. The figure numbers the box office's parts in the order the walk adds them.

The same walk finds loops. Keep a path: the components you're inside right now. If you reach one that's already on the path, you've come back to a card that is still waiting for its own needs. Picture three cards that point in a circle: the rota of who works which night needs the cast list, the cast list needs the rehearsal plan, and the rehearsal plan needs the rota. The container reports the slice of the path from the repeated class back to itself:

Dependency cycle: Rota -> CastList -> RehearsalPlan -> Rota

Here the manager picture breaks, in a useful way. A manager can improvise when a card is unclear or two cards point at each other, and often gets away with it. A container that improvises, picking a constructor or breaking a loop by guessing, builds a program nobody wrote. So the lab's container reads every card in its own constructor, before it builds a single part.

A container should refuse a card it can't read, before the doors open. Check the whole graph when the container is created.

A missing part, a doubtful constructor or a loop then stops the program as it starts, with a message, instead of at the first ticket of the night. Building the parts can still wait until someone asks for them, and that's where the last flaw lives.

try.title: Predict the order, then make a loop
steps: Read GraphDemo. The scan returns the components in name order, and the walk starts from each one in turn. Write down the creation order you expect for all nine.
Run it and compare. Then run the Kotlin twin, which ends with two refusals.
In app/SalesBook.java, change the constructor to public SalesBook(BoxOffice office) {}. Predict the message, then run GraphDemo again. Undo the change afterwards.

code.title: GraphDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.container.l01.demo; import workbench.container.l01.Container; import workbench.container.l01.ContainerException; import workbench.container.l01.demo.app.BoxOffice; import java.util.List; /** Wires the demo app from a scan, prints the creation order, then tries a graph with a cycle. */ public class GraphDemo { public static class Rota { public Rota(CastList cast) {} } // who works which night public static class CastList { public CastList(RehearsalPlan rehearsals) {} } public static class RehearsalPlan { public RehearsalPlan(Rota rota) {} } public static void main(String[] args) { Container app = Container.scan("workbench.container.l01.demo.app"); System.out.println("creation order: " + app.creationOrder().stream().map(Class::getSimpleName).toList()); app.get(BoxOffice.class).sell("C12", 12_000); try { new Container(List.of(Rota.class, CastList.class, RehearsalPlan.class)); } catch (ContainerException e) { System.out.println("cycle: " + e.getMessage()); } } }

alt.title: GraphDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.container.l01.demo import workbench.container.l01.Container import workbench.container.l01.ContainerException import workbench.container.l01.Inject // The same wiring with Kotlin classes, a cycle, and Kotlin's extra constructors. class GSeatingPlan class GPriceList(val plan: GSeatingPlan) class GSalesBook class GBoxOffice(val prices: GPriceList, val book: GSalesBook) class GRota(val cast: GCastList) class GCastList(val rehearsals: GRehearsalPlan) class GRehearsalPlan(val rota: GRota) class GPriceRules @Inject constructor(val feePercent: Int = 3) // every parameter has a default fun main() { val app = Container(listOf(GBoxOffice::class.java, GSalesBook::class.java, GPriceList::class.java, GSeatingPlan::class.java)) println("creation order: " + app.creationOrder().map { it.simpleName }) println("same PriceList: " + (app.get(GBoxOffice::class.java).prices === app.get(GPriceList::class.java))) for (components in listOf(listOf(GRota::class.java, GCastList::class.java, GRehearsalPlan::class.java), listOf(GPriceRules::class.java))) { try { Container(components) } catch (e: ContainerException) { println("refused: ${e.message}") } } }

try.expect: The order is [AttendanceLog, BookingConfig, RemoteBookingClient, SeatingPlan, PriceList, SalesBook, BoxOffice, TicketArchive, ClosingJob]. BookingConfig comes second because AttendanceLog needs nothing, and the walk reaches BookingConfig from BoxOffice through RemoteBookingClient. Neither static initializer prints, because nobody asked for ClosingJob. The Java run ends with cycle: Dependency cycle: Rota -> CastList -> RehearsalPlan -> Rota. The Kotlin twin prints refused: Dependency cycle: GRota -> GCastList -> GRehearsalPlan -> GRota and refused: GPriceRules has 2 @Inject constructors; keep one. With your change, the scan itself throws ContainerException: Dependency cycle: BoxOffice -> SalesBook -> BoxOffice.

sections.h: Build each shared part once, even when eight threads ask first
sections.html:
A singleton component has one instance per container, created the first time someone asks for it: the one seating plan. A prototype component is created again on every request, like a fresh basket for each customer at the box office. Singleton is the default, and it's where the bugs live, because the first request often arrives on several threads at once. (A thread is one path of work running beside others in the same program.) When the doors open, eight customers can reach the box office in the same second.

The obvious memory for our ten lines is a map from class to instance: look the class up, and build the part only if it's missing. That's check-then-act, the race from Race conditions: why count++ lies. Every thread that reads null before the first put builds a plan of its own. The demo releases eight threads at once on a SeatingPlan that takes 20 ms to read the hall's map:

check-then-act on a map  constructor ran 8 times, threads saw 8 instance(s)

Eight customers, eight seating plans. ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent looks like the fix, because it builds a missing value atomically, in one step that no other thread can split. But a container calls it recursively: building BoxOffice means building SalesBook first, from inside the function that builds BoxOffice. The Javadoc forbids that; the function must not change the map. In practice the result depends on luck. The map keeps its entries in numbered buckets called bins, chosen from each key's hash code. Two keys in different bins work. Two in the same bin throw:

computeIfAbsent, boxOffice needs priceList: worked
computeIfAbsent, boxOffice needs salesBook: java.lang.IllegalStateException: Recursive update

With Class keys, the hash code changes from run to run, so the same container would fail on some starts and not on others. Nobody wants to debug that on opening night.

The JVM has a lazy singleton of its own: the holder idiom from Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders. A nested class keeps the instance in a static final field, and the JVM sets that field in the class's dress rehearsal, once, under the class initialization lock. It's the best tool when you can write one holder class per singleton before you compile. A reflective container can't, because it learns its components only when the program runs. Lesson 3 of this track generates those holder classes.

So the lab gives each singleton a small cell that uses double-checked locking. In that lesson's shop, two assistants saw the stockroom door shut and both went to open it. The fix was to look, and only if the door is shut, take the key and look again:

Java
T value = instance;                      // volatile read: no lock once it's built
if (value == null) {
    synchronized (this) {
        value = instance;                // someone may have built it while we waited
        if (value == null) instance = value = factory.get();
    }
}
return value;
Kotlin
var value = instance                     // @Volatile var instance: T? = null
if (value == null) {
    synchronized(this) {
        value = instance                 // someone may have built it while we waited
        if (value == null) { value = factory(); instance = value }
    }
}
return value!!

volatile is what makes the first, unlocked read safe. A thread that reads a non-null reference also sees every write the constructor made before the reference was stored. Without it, a thread could see the reference and still read the new object's fields as zero: the stockroom door open, the lights still off. In the demo, the cell ran the constructor once, and all eight threads saw one instance.

You may worry about the locks. Building BoxOffice holds its cell's lock while it builds PriceList, which takes another cell's lock. Nested locks usually bring a risk of deadlock: two threads each waiting for a lock the other holds. Deadlock, livelock and starvation showed that such a freeze needs the waits to form a loop. Here every lock is taken along an arrow of the graph, from a component to something it needs, and the container has already refused loops. One more difference from a holder: if the constructor throws, the cell stays empty and the next get tries again. A dress rehearsal that fails is a failure for good, and the class answers NoClassDefFoundError from then on.

try.title: Race for the first seating plan
steps: Read SingletonRaceDemo (or the Kotlin twin). Each row releases eight threads at the same moment, and SeatingPlan takes 20 ms to build.
Predict the two numbers on each of the first two rows, and which computeIfAbsent line fails.
Run it twice. Do the numbers change?

code.title: SingletonRaceDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.container.l01.demo; import workbench.container.l01.SingletonCell; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.IdentityHashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.Set; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** Eight threads ask for the same singleton at the same moment, three ways. */ public class SingletonRaceDemo { static final AtomicInteger CONSTRUCTED = new AtomicInteger(); public static class SeatingPlan { public SeatingPlan() { CONSTRUCTED.incrementAndGet(); try { Thread.sleep(20); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } // reads the hall's map } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Map<Class<?>, Object> beans = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); race("check-then-act on a map", () -> { Object bean = beans.get(SeatingPlan.class); // check if (bean == null) { bean = new SeatingPlan(); // act: every thread that saw null gets here beans.put(SeatingPlan.class, bean); } return bean; }); SingletonCell<SeatingPlan> cell = new SingletonCell<>(SeatingPlan::new); race("SingletonCell", cell::get); // computeIfAbsent can't build a graph: the function must not touch the same map for (String[] edge : new String[][] {{"boxOffice", "priceList"}, {"boxOffice", "salesBook"}}) { Map<String, Object> byName = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); try { byName.computeIfAbsent(edge[0], k -> List.of(byName.computeIfAbsent(edge[1], k2 -> new Object()))); System.out.printf("computeIfAbsent, %s needs %s: worked%n", edge[0], edge[1]); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.printf("computeIfAbsent, %s needs %s: %s%n", edge[0], edge[1], e); } } } static void race(String name, Supplier<Object> get) throws InterruptedException { CONSTRUCTED.set(0); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Set<Object> seen = java.util.Collections.synchronizedSet(java.util.Collections.newSetFromMap(new IdentityHashMap<>())); List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } seen.add(get.get()); }); t.start(); threads.add(t); } go.countDown(); // all eight start together for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); System.out.printf("%-24s constructor ran %d times, threads saw %d instance(s)%n", name, CONSTRUCTED.get(), seen.size()); } }

alt.title: SingletonRaceDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.container.l01.demo import workbench.container.l01.SingletonCell import java.util.Collections import java.util.IdentityHashMap import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Eight threads ask for the same singleton at the same moment, three ways. private val constructed = AtomicInteger() class RaceSeatingPlan { init { constructed.incrementAndGet() Thread.sleep(20) // reads the hall's map } } fun main() { val beans = ConcurrentHashMap<Class<*>, Any>() race("check-then-act on a map") { beans[RaceSeatingPlan::class.java] ?: RaceSeatingPlan().also { beans[RaceSeatingPlan::class.java] = it } // check, then act } val cell = SingletonCell { RaceSeatingPlan() } race("SingletonCell") { cell.get() } // computeIfAbsent can't build a graph: the function must not touch the same map for ((outer, inner) in listOf("boxOffice" to "priceList", "boxOffice" to "salesBook")) { val byName = ConcurrentHashMap<String, Any>() try { byName.computeIfAbsent(outer) { listOf(byName.computeIfAbsent(inner) { Any() }) } println("computeIfAbsent, $outer needs $inner: worked") } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("computeIfAbsent, $outer needs $inner: $e") } } } private fun race(name: String, get: () -> Any) { constructed.set(0) val go = CountDownLatch(1) val seen = Collections.synchronizedSet(Collections.newSetFromMap(IdentityHashMap<Any, Boolean>())) val threads = List(8) { thread { go.await() seen += get() } } go.countDown() // all eight start together threads.forEach { it.join() } println("%-24s constructor ran %d times, threads saw %d instance(s)".format(name, constructed.get(), seen.size)) }

try.expect: check-then-act on a map constructor ran 8 times, threads saw 8 instance(s) (now and then slightly fewer), then SingletonCell ... 1 times ... 1 instance(s) on every run. boxOffice needs priceList: worked, but boxOffice needs salesBook: java.lang.IllegalStateException: Recursive update, because those two strings land in the same bin of a 16-bin table. Change either name and the result may flip, which is exactly why nobody should rely on it.

compare.title: The same component in Java and Kotlin, as reflection sees it

java.title: PriceList.java
java.html: @Component public class PriceList { private final SeatingPlan plan; private final int feePercent; @Inject // two public constructors: say which one public PriceList(SeatingPlan plan) { this(plan, 3); } public PriceList(SeatingPlan plan, int feePercent) { this.plan = plan; this.feePercent = feePercent; } } // getConstructors(): (SeatingPlan) and (SeatingPlan, int). No synthetic ones.

kotlin.title: PriceList.kt
kotlin.html: @Component class PriceList(private val plan: SeatingPlan, private val feePercent: Int = 3) // getConstructors(): // PriceList(SeatingPlan, int) // PriceList(SeatingPlan, int, int, DefaultConstructorMarker) synthetic, skip it // The container picks (SeatingPlan, int), then finds no component for int. // Give feePercent no default, or move it into a FeeRules component.

compare.note: Java gives you exactly the constructors you write. Kotlin compiles default arguments into an extra public synthetic constructor, and if every parameter has a default, into a real no-argument constructor as well, which receives the same annotations. So a container must filter isSynthetic() and must not be fooled by an @Inject that kotlinc copied. In both languages the class file keeps no parameter names by default, so the container matches by type. The Kotlin class is also final, which is harmless here and becomes the main problem in lesson 2.

worked.title: Break a loop the container reported

steps.say: The container refuses to start with Dependency cycle: BoxOffice -> SeatFinder -> BoxOffice. Here are the two classes. Read them and ask what each one needs while it's being built, and what it only needs later, inside a method.
steps.code: @Component public class BoxOffice { private final SoldSeats sold = new SoldSeats(); // hidden inside private final SeatFinder finder; public BoxOffice(SeatFinder finder) { this.finder = finder; } public String sellBestSeat() { String seat = finder.bestFreeSeat(); sold.add(seat); return seat; } public boolean isSold(String seat) { return sold.contains(seat); } } @Component public class SeatFinder { private final BoxOffice office; public SeatFinder(BoxOffice office) { this.office = office; } public String bestFreeSeat() { return SEATS.stream().filter(s -> !office.isSold(s)).findFirst().orElseThrow(); } }

alt.html: @Component class BoxOffice(private val finder: SeatFinder) { private val sold = SoldSeats() // hidden inside fun sellBestSeat(): String = finder.bestFreeSeat().also { sold.add(it) } fun isSold(seat: String): Boolean = sold.contains(seat) } @Component class SeatFinder(private val office: BoxOffice) { fun bestFreeSeat(): String = SEATS.first { !office.isSold(it) } }

steps.say: SeatFinder doesn't need a BoxOffice at all. It needs to know which seats are sold, and that list lives in SoldSeats, hidden inside BoxOffice. BoxOffice needs the list to write to and the finder to ask. The loop exists only because the list is hidden.
Give the list its own component. Both classes depend on it, and the arrows no longer close a loop: SoldSeats is created first, then SeatFinder, then BoxOffice.
steps.code: @Component public class SoldSeats { private final Set<String> seats = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(); public void add(String seat) { seats.add(seat); } public boolean contains(String seat) { return seats.contains(seat); } } @Component public class SeatFinder { private final SoldSeats sold; public SeatFinder(SoldSeats sold) { this.sold = sold; } public String bestFreeSeat() { return SEATS.stream().filter(s -> !sold.contains(s)).findFirst().orElseThrow(); } } @Component public class BoxOffice { private final SoldSeats sold; private final SeatFinder finder; public BoxOffice(SoldSeats sold, SeatFinder finder) { this.sold = sold; this.finder = finder; } public String sellBestSeat() { String seat = finder.bestFreeSeat(); sold.add(seat); return seat; } }

alt.html: @Component class SoldSeats { private val seats = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet<String>() fun add(seat: String) { seats += seat } fun contains(seat: String): Boolean = seat in seats } @Component class SeatFinder(private val sold: SoldSeats) { fun bestFreeSeat(): String = SEATS.first { !sold.contains(it) } } @Component class BoxOffice(private val sold: SoldSeats, private val finder: SeatFinder) { fun sellBestSeat(): String = finder.bestFreeSeat().also { sold.add(it) } }

steps.say: If two parts really do need each other at call time, real containers offer a lookup instead of an object: jakarta.inject.Provider<BoxOffice> in the Jakarta standard, ObjectProvider<BoxOffice> in Spring. The constructor then receives something that finds the BoxOffice later, inside a method. The lab's container doesn't offer that, on purpose. Reach for it after you've tried the split, not before.

lab.title: Write the four decisive parts of the container
steps: Run the tests once. Eleven of twelve fail with UnsupportedOperationException. The one that passes tests ClassScanner, which is given: read it once, because it's section 2 in code. The test fixtures are a small box office in src/test/java/.../l01/app.

Write Constructors.pick. Filter getConstructors() with !c.isSynthetic(), then apply the three rules from its Javadoc. The tests check the exact messages, including two Kotlin classes from KotlinBeans.kt.

Write BeanGraph.creationOrder as a depth-first, post-order walk. Keep a Set of finished classes and a LinkedHashSet path of the classes you're inside. Build the cycle message from the part of the path that starts at the repeated class.
Write SingletonCell.get with double-checked locking on the volatile field.

Write Container.create: pick the constructor, map graph.dependenciesOf(component) through instanceOf, and call newInstance. Then write instanceOf: the cell's get() for singletons, create for prototypes. Run the tests until all twelve pass, then twice more.
hints: In creationOrder, check done before path. A finished class is not a loop, even when two components both depend on it.
A recursive helper visit(c, done, path, order) keeps the main method to three lines. Add c to path before visiting its dependencies, and remove it after.

Constructor.newInstance wraps whatever the constructor throws in InvocationTargetException. The test wants the original IllegalStateException as the cause of your ContainerException: use e.getCause().
If the concurrency test sees two SlowPlans, you read instance once outside the lock but not again inside it.
lab.done: All twelve tests in WiringTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Order a graph from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Given Map<String, List<String>> needs (component name to the names its constructor needs), write List<String> creationOrder(Map<String, List<String>> needs) that returns each name after everything it needs, and throws IllegalStateException("cycle: a -> b -> a") on a loop. Then compare with the answer. Did you check done before the path?

answer.html: static List<String> creationOrder(Map<String, List<String>> needs) { List<String> order = new ArrayList<>(); Set<String> done = new HashSet<>(); for (String name : needs.keySet()) visit(name, needs, done, new LinkedHashSet<>(), order); return order; } static void visit(String name, Map<String, List<String>> needs, Set<String> done, LinkedHashSet<String> path, List<String> order) { if (done.contains(name)) return; // finished earlier: not a loop if (path.contains(name)) { // back at a name we are still inside List<String> loop = new ArrayList<>(path); loop = loop.subList(loop.indexOf(name), loop.size()); throw new IllegalStateException("cycle: " + String.join(" -> ", loop) + " -> " + name); } path.add(name); for (String dep : needs.getOrDefault(name, List.of())) visit(dep, needs, done, path, order); path.remove(name); done.add(name); order.add(name); // after everything it needs }

alt.html: fun creationOrder(needs: Map<String, List<String>>): List<String> { val order = mutableListOf<String>() val done = mutableSetOf<String>() val path = linkedSetOf<String>() fun visit(name: String) { if (name in done) return // finished earlier: not a loop if (name in path) { // back at a name we are still inside val loop = path.dropWhile { it != name } + name throw IllegalStateException("cycle: " + loop.joinToString(" -> ")) } path += name needs[name].orEmpty().forEach(::visit) path -= name done += name order += name // after everything it needs } needs.keys.forEach(::visit) return order }

recap: A container does the wiring block of main for you, the way a front-of-house manager reads each desk's card: it finds the components, builds each one from its constructor, and decides how many of each exist.

A scan asks a class loader for the package's directory and loads each class with Class.forName(name, false, loader), so no static initializer runs. @Component needs @Retention(RUNTIME), every scanned class is loaded on every start, and a JAR without directory entries scans as empty.
Pick the @Inject constructor or the only public one, never "the first". Skip Kotlin's synthetic constructors, don't give injected parameters defaults, and match parameters by type.
Create components in depth-first post-order, and keep a path to find loops. Check the whole graph when the container is created, so a broken card stops the start, not the first sale.

A singleton is one instance per container. Check-then-act on a map builds duplicates, and a recursive computeIfAbsent can throw Recursive update. A cell with double-checked locking on a volatile field builds exactly one, and can't deadlock on a graph without loops.
Where today's container stops: it hands out plain objects. It can't time a call or try it again when the booking service doesn't answer; lesson 2 puts proxies around the parts.

explain.prompt: A colleague asks why the container's constructor walks the whole graph when it could simply create things on the first get. Explain what the walk gives you, what still happens lazily, and why the two together are a good trade.
explain.answer: The walk only reads constructors and matches types, so it's cheap. It proves at start-up that every dependency has exactly one provider, that every class has a constructor the container can call, and that there are no loops, and it produces the creation order. A broken graph then stops the program as it starts, with a clear message, instead of failing the first request that happens to touch the bad part. What stays lazy is running the constructors: a singleton is built on first use, inside its cell, so the start doesn't pay for components nobody uses. The cost of the trade is that a constructor that throws still surprises you on first use, which is why constructors should only store their arguments.

deeper.html:
Spring creates its singletons eagerly at the end of start-up by default, after the scan and the graph work, so that a constructor that throws stops the start too. The lab's container is lazy, like a CDI client proxy (CDI is the Jakarta standard for dependency injection), which creates its bean on the first method call. Neither is wrong; they put the same failure at different times.

Spring can also resolve some loops that the lab refuses. With field or setter injection, it can hand out a reference to an object whose constructor has finished but whose fields aren't all set yet, from a cache of "early" singleton references. Constructor injection can never do that, because the object doesn't exist until its constructor's arguments do. That's one reason constructor injection is the recommended style: an impossible graph fails loudly. Since Spring Boot 2.6, even the setter-injection kind of loop is refused unless you set spring.main.allow-circular-references=true.

Three things a production container adds to this lesson's graph. Qualifiers, for when two components implement the same interface and the injection point must say which (@Named, @Qualifier). Generic types, so that Repository<Show> and Repository<Seat> are different dependencies (the lab compares erased classes only). And lookups such as Provider<T>, which turn a hard edge into one that is followed at call time. Each one makes the graph work harder, and each one is easier to check at build time than at start-up, which is where lesson 3 of this track ends up.
